guide.label: Learning path
guide.wait: The next chapter “{next}” opens as soon as the game gets there. Just keep playing.
guide.erstesSpiel.title: Your first game
guide.erstesSpiel.text: A game is a combination of genre, theme, platform and cards. Everything is preselected sensibly. The preview below shows live how well genre and theme fit and what score to expect.
guide.zeit.title: Let time run
guide.zeit.text: The speed buttons are at the bottom (space = pause/resume). Your team works week by week. Important moments pause the game on their own, and decisions appear on the right.
guide.zeit.goal: Let a few weeks pass until the project shows progress.
guide.playtest.title: Playtest
guide.playtest.text: A playtest costs a week and shows the expected score and weaknesses. With “Change course” you can still swap cards afterwards.
guide.playtest.goal: Run a playtest on the project.
guide.release.title: Release
guide.release.text: Once the game is finished, every extra week finds bugs but costs wages. When the bug curve flattens, it is a good moment. The release package sets price, print run and distribution; the autopilot picks sensibly.
guide.wertung.title: Understand the score
guide.wertung.text: The score comes from cards times team times fit times engine, minus bugs, measured against the press expectation. The knowledge book shows the full chain, and each game shows which part cost the most.
guide.wertung.goal: Make your second game better than the first and release it.
guide.wachsen.title: Grow
guide.wachsen.text: Applications now appear as decisions. Look at strength in the area your genre lacks and at the salary: wages are your largest cost.
guide.marketing.title: Marketing
guide.marketing.text: Marketing builds interest; interest at release turns into sales in the first weeks. The slider is a share of development costs. Announcing early pays off, too early fizzles out.
guide.marketing.goal: Set a marketing budget for a running project.
guide.auftraege.title: Contracts
guide.auftraege.text: Contracts bring safe money between your own games: single jobs bind one person, contract games a whole project with requirements and a minimum score. Brand and sales of a contract game belong to the client.
guide.auftraege.goal: Accept a contract or a contract game.
guide.engine.title: Your own engine
guide.engine.text: Many cards need a tech level. An own engine costs staff, but raises the engine factor of all games and can be licensed later.
guide.engine.goal: Found your own engine (or skip the chapter on purpose).
guide.teams.title: Teams
guide.teams.text: From 8 people you can form teams. In the people list, filter by area, select several and form a team. A specialist team is 10 % better in its area; a QA team finds bugs in all projects.
guide.teams.goal: Form a team and give it a focus.
guide.groesser.title: Bigger projects
guide.groesser.text: Medium projects have more card slots and more demand, but need more staff and have a gate after pre-production. Large comes in 1990, AAA in 1998.
guide.marken.title: Brands
guide.marken.text: A successful game becomes a brand with fans. A sequel starts with those fans, but too many entries in a row tire them.
guide.marken.goal: Release a sequel in one of your brands.
unlock.label: New area
unlock.auftraege.what: Other companies offer contracts: one person works a few weeks for money. After your first release there are also contract games with requirements and a minimum score.
unlock.auftraege.when: people are idle or money is getting tight.
unlock.auftraege.cost: The person is missing from your own projects; contract games bring no own brand.
unlock.bewerbungen.what: Applications arrive as decisions. Each person has strengths per area and a salary.
unlock.bewerbungen.when: your genre lacks an area or projects take too long.
unlock.bewerbungen.cost: Monthly salary; more people need more office seats.
unlock.zeitleiste.what: The timeline shows which platforms launch and phase out.
unlock.zeitleiste.when: you plan for the next platform.
unlock.zeitleiste.cost: Nothing, it is just an overview.
unlock.markt.what: The market view shows competitors, rankings and trends of genres and themes.
unlock.markt.when: you plan a new game: trends raise or lower sales.
unlock.markt.cost: Nothing, it is just an overview.
unlock.produkttypen.what: Besides new games you can make ports (same game, new platform) and add-ons for your games.
unlock.produkttypen.when: a game did well: ports and add-ons are quick and cheap.
unlock.produkttypen.cost: Less impact than a new game; add-ons only sell to owners.
unlock.engine.what: You can found your own engine. Its modules unlock better cards and raise the engine factor.
unlock.engine.when: you lack cards the starter engine cannot do.
unlock.engine.cost: People in the engine team do not work on games.
unlock.marken.what: Successful games become brands with fans. Sequels start with those fans.
unlock.marken.cost: Too many entries in a row tire the fans.
unlock.firma.what: Your studio is growing: the company view bundles staff, teams, staff policy and office.
unlock.firma.when: you run several projects at once.
unlock.firma.cost: Nothing; teams and specialist teams are a matter of organisation.
unlock.betrieb.what: Online games need operations: servers, support, patches and community.
unlock.betrieb.when: you run live games or MMOs.
unlock.betrieb.cost: Running costs for servers and staff.
unlock.publisher.what: Publishers fund projects in exchange for a share of revenue.
unlock.publisher.when: a project is bigger than your bank account.
unlock.publisher.cost: Part of the revenue until the advance is recouped, plus milestone pressure.
unlock.standorte.what: Further locations in other regions: different wages, subsidies and taxes.
unlock.standorte.when: the office is full or wages are cheaper elsewhere.
unlock.standorte.cost: Deposit, ramp-up time at half output, leadership effort.
unlock.delegation.what: Producers run projects, rules answer recurring decisions for you.
unlock.delegation.cost: Producers are missing from development; rules do not always decide like you.
unlock.lizenzmarkt.what: Other studios ask for your engine, or you license someone else's.
unlock.lizenzmarkt.when: your engine is good (income) or your own lags behind.

hb.title: Handbook
hb.intro: Short articles on every area. The map shows how everything connects; click a box to open its article.
hb.karten.title: Cards (features)
hb.karten.what: Cards are the content of your game. Each belongs to an area (gameplay, graphics, sound, story, tech) and has a value.
hb.karten.how: Sum of card values, boosted by synergies between cards and by the fit to the profile the press expects for the genre.
hb.karten.mistakes: Taking only the most valuable cards even if they skew the profile; cards the engine cannot do.
hb.karten.where: Projects → New project; each card's tooltip shows value, effort, synergies and requirements.
hb.team.title: Team
hb.team.what: Who works on the game decides how well the cards are executed and how fast it gets done.
hb.team.how: For each card the best person in its area counts, plus experience with genre and engine. Specialist teams +10 % in their focus, −10 % elsewhere. More people = faster, but not linear.
hb.team.mistakes: Putting everyone on one project and then having nobody for the next; crunching too long (burnout).
hb.team.where: Company or Projects → people list with filters and multi-select; teams below.
hb.engine.title: Engine
hb.engine.what: The technology behind your games. Its modules decide which cards are possible and give the engine factor.
hb.engine.how: Engine factor = your modules against the state of the art of the year. An old engine drags every score down.
hb.engine.mistakes: Starting an own engine too late; research without a plan; a new major version in the middle of production.
hb.engine.where: Engine view (after the 2nd release or from 1982).
hb.passung.title: Fit: genre, theme, audience
hb.passung.what: Some combinations fit (fantasy RPG), others do not (cooking shooter). The audience sets market size, loyalty and press strictness.
hb.passung.how: Genre–theme fit acts directly on the score (0.5 to 1.3). Trends raise or lower sales. Each audience has genres that suit it.
hb.passung.mistakes: Chasing a trend despite poor fit; children as the audience with content rated 2 or higher.
hb.passung.where: New project (▲▼ on genre and theme, audience with effects) and knowledge book (what you have found out).
hb.bugs.title: Bugs and testing
hb.bugs.what: Bugs appear during work and lower the score if they are still in at release.
hb.bugs.how: After production ends, the team finds a share of the bugs each week; the curve flattens. A QA team finds more in all projects. Crunch creates more bugs.
hb.bugs.mistakes: Releasing right when the game is done; testing too long once the curve is flat.
hb.bugs.where: Project card: bug curve and release button.
hb.wertung.title: Score
hb.wertung.what: The press score from 1 to 10. It decides how many people buy your game and for how long.
hb.wertung.how: Quality (cards × synergy × profile × team × engine × fit × (1 − bugs)) divided by the press expectation. The expectation rises every year with the industry's games and depends on scope and audience.
hb.wertung.mistakes: Making the same combination for years: the expectation grows, your score falls.
hb.wertung.where: After release: breakdown in the project; before: preview on the board and playtest.
hb.verkauf.title: Sales and marketing
hb.verkauf.what: Score, interest and market turn into sales.
hb.verkauf.how: Launch sales = interest at release + impulse buyers from the platform base, times trend, season and competition. Then the curve falls; a good score and loyal audiences slow the drop. Marketing builds interest.
hb.verkauf.mistakes: Too small a print run (sold out) or too large (storage costs); releasing in the same week as a big competitor.
hb.verkauf.where: Project card (marketing), release package (price, print run, distribution), knowledge book → products.
hb.geld.title: Money and finances
hb.geld.what: Wages and rent run every week; income comes in waves after each release.
hb.geld.how: Cash = income (sales, contracts, licenses) − costs (wages, rent, production, marketing, taxes). Loans bridge gaps but cost interest. Several months in the red lead to insolvency.
hb.geld.mistakes: Hiring too fast; betting everything on one big game without a cushion.
hb.geld.where: Finances view with monthly overview; cash at the top with trend arrow.
hb.umfang.title: Scope: small to AAA
hb.umfang.what: Scope decides card slots, effort, phases and market.
hb.umfang.how: Small 3 cards (effort ×0.4), medium 5 (×1), large 7 (×2.5, from 1990), AAA 9 (×5, from 1998). From medium there is a gate with continue, change course, pause or cancel; large and AAA have a vertical slice.
hb.umfang.mistakes: Going big without enough staff: the project takes years and the tech gets old.
hb.auftraege.title: Contracts and contract games
hb.auftraege.what: Safe money between your own games.
hb.auftraege.how: Single jobs bind one person for weeks and pay by quality. Contract games are whole projects with requirements: advance at start, remainder from the minimum score, bonus from +1.0, otherwise penalty. Brand and sales belong to the client.
hb.auftraege.mistakes: Accepting a contract game whose minimum score your team cannot reach; missing the deadline.
hb.auftraege.where: Projects → contract games (below the projects); single jobs arrive as decisions.
hb.marken.title: Brands
hb.marken.what: Successful games become brands with fans.
hb.marken.how: A sequel starts with the brand's fans. Hits strengthen it, flops hurt. Too many entries in a row tire fans; a break restores them.
hb.wachstum.title: Growth: publishers, IPO, acquisitions
hb.wachstum.what: Ways to more capital and more studios.
hb.wachstum.how: Publishers fund a project for a revenue share. The IPO (from 2000, 60 people) brings capital but quarterly pressure. Acquisitions buy whole studios that you run as subsidiaries with directives.
hb.wachstum.mistakes: Buying a studio whose culture does not fit; more subsidiaries than integration capacity.
hb.loop: The loop closes: money pays for staff, engine and office, which make the next game better.
first.label: First time
first.gate.title: Your first gate
first.gate.text: From medium scope on, the project stops after the concept. This is the cheapest moment to change course or cancel: every change costs more later.
first.freeze.title: Engine frozen
first.freeze.text: Past a certain progress the project uses the engine as it is now. New modules only help the next game; switching costs weeks.
first.crunch.title: Crunch on
first.crunch.text: Crunch makes the team faster but creates more bugs and exhaustion. Shortly before gold it sometimes pays off, as a permanent state never.
first.minus.title: Cash in the red
first.minus.text: A few weeks in the red are no drama; several months lead to insolvency. A contract, a loan or an earlier release closes the gap.
mentor.saeulen: The cards did not deliver what the design pillars promised. Pick pillars your cards fit, or leave them out.
hb.saeulen.title: Design pillars
hb.saeulen.what: Up to two pillars say what your game stands for: innovation, accessibility, depth, presentation or content.
hb.saeulen.how: For each pillar the share of card value with matching tags counts. From 40 % you get the full bonus (up to +5 %, times the press preference in the genre); below 15 % a 4 % penalty.
hb.saeulen.mistakes: Choosing pillars that do not suit the genre (▼), or pillars without matching cards.
hb.saeulen.where: New project → design pillars; matching cards carry a ◆.
hb.phasen.title: Focus per phase
hb.phasen.what: For pre-production, production and beta you decide whether the team works faster, more thoroughly or with fewer bugs.
hb.phasen.how: Pace affects output, bugs affect new bugs in that phase. Quality counts by share of work: thorough pre-production (×1.2) affects about a seventh of the work, polish (×1.06) more than half. Both land in the “team” bar.
hb.phasen.mistakes: Choosing speed everywhere and then not getting rid of the bugs in beta; bug hunting a project that has few bugs.
hb.phasen.where: Project card → focus per phase (from medium scope with all three phases).
hb.politur.title: Polish per area
hb.politur.what: After production the team can polish one area instead of only hunting bugs.
hb.politur.how: Each week polish closes 15 % of the gap to +15 % on the value of all cards in that area: the first weeks bring the most. In those weeks the team finds only half as many bugs. The bonus shows in the “team” bar.
hb.politur.mistakes: Polishing an area with few cards; polishing for weeks while the bugs stay in.
hb.lokalisierung.title: Localization
hb.lokalisierung.what: Translations open more language markets for your game.
hb.lokalisierung.how: Each language market has a share of sales that changes over the years (Chinese growing strongly from 2000). Without translation it buys only 10 to 40 %. Costs depend on scope and amount of text and are due at release.
hb.lokalisierung.mistakes: Translating a small, text-heavy game into every language; leaving out Japanese although the market is large.
scenario.indieDurchbruch.text: 2015, five people in a small office floor, little reputation and money for about a year. The big studios own the headlines.
scenario.indieDurchbruch.goal: Goal: release a game of your own with at least 500,000 interested players at launch by the end of {year}.
scenario.konzernIntegration.text: 2020, a group of 30 people has just bought three studios at once. Integration overwhelms management, and people at the subsidiaries are already looking for new jobs.
scenario.konzernIntegration.goal: Goal: fully integrate all three subsidiaries by the end of {year} with at most two departures. Closing or losing a subsidiary loses the scenario.

unlock.saeulen.when: the team is big enough to commit to a direction.
unlock.saeulen.cost: Cards outside the pillars count less.
roadmap.desc.saeulen: Up to three design pillars that carry the project.
